newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reformer wins regional vote, Kremlin happy.
newsitem.headline: Russian reformer wins regional vote, Kremlin happy.

text.p: Kremlin-backed reformist Ivan Sklyarov defeated a communist rival to become governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region in an election seen as a litmus test for liberal reforms.

The election commission said on Monday that Sklyarov, the 49-year-old mayor of Nizhny Novgorod city, had won 52 percent of the votes in Sunday's election. Communist Gennady Khodyrev, who ran the region then known as Gorky under Soviet rule, received 42 percent. Turnout was 49 percent.
"This was a regional election of national importance," political analyst Vladimir Okmyansky told local television.

"In all previous elections, results in Nizhny Novgorod differed by only one percent or so from the (average) results for Russia as a whole. Victory by the 'party of power' over the region's communist opposition can be seen as showing the balance of forces on the national scene."

The outcome was a relief for the Kremlin after a tough campaign battle since a first round election two weeks ago in which the two candidates emerged as the front-runners but neither won enough votes for an outright victory.

The result overshadowed a disappointment for the Kremlin on Sunday in the central city of Samara, formerly Kuybyshev, where a supporter of outspoken General Alexander Lebed was elected mayor -- a post which holds less power than a regional governor.

Georgy Limansky, head of the regional branch of a party led by Lebed, won more than 54 percent of the votes compared to the 38 percent cast for Kremlin-backed Anatoly Afanasyev. The result will encourage Lebed, a fierce critic of President Boris Yeltsin who is expected to run for president in the year 2000.
The election in Nizhny Novgorod, 420 km (260 miles) east of Moscow, filled the post vacated by reformer Boris Nemtsov when Yeltsin summoned him to Moscow in March.
Nemtsov, who was appointed a first deputy prime minister, is now overseeing radical economic and welfare reforms, some of which he tried out in Nizhny Novgorod during six years in power.
Nemtsov congratulated Sklyarov after the provisional results had been announced, Interfax news agency said.
"Sklyarov's success is a victory of common sense, a victory of constructive, healthy forces in the society over political extremists," the agency quoted Nemtsov's spokesman as saying.

"The people of Nizhny Novgorod have proved that they want to enter the 21st century living in a democratic society with a developed socially-oriented market economy, without turning back to empty communist slogans and ideals," he added.
A communist victory in his former domain would have provided powerful ammunition for the opponents of reforms.

It would also have been an embarrassment for Nemtsov, posing questions about the depth of support for his reforms in Nizhny Novgorod. Nemtsov, a potential presidential candidate, and other government leaders had campaigned hard for Sklyarov.
Their open support highlighted the importance of the vote in the region of four million people on the Volga river.
Communist leaders, backed by ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, also visited the region to campaign for Khodyrev, the region's communist chief in the late 1980s.
Valentin Kuptsov, a senior communist leader in Moscow, said the election had been close and showed that society was divided over the government's painful reforms.
"The outcome again shows to what extent society is split. The 52-42 result shows half of society is in opposition to the authorities and are not happy with their course," he said.
Khodyrev did not comment on the outcome but told local television he was not planning to challenge the results.
